label: Forward P/E
description: Price relative to expected next-year earnings; sourced from ticker.info forwardPE.
calculation: Share price ÷ forecast earnings per share for next year (Yahoo forwardPE).
interpretation: Higher = the market pays more per dollar of expected profit (priced for quality/growth, or simply expensive). Always read next to growth.
applicability: Undefined for loss-makers (negative or near-zero forecast earnings): the value is meaningless, not "cheap."
analogy: Think payback time: how many years of expected earnings are priced into one share today.
learn: P/E (price-to-earnings) divides the share price by earnings per share. Forward P/E uses analyst estimates for next year's earnings, not last year's results. A higher number often means investors expect faster growth, or are paying a premium today. A lower number can mean the stock is genuinely cheap, or that investors expect slower growth ahead.

label: Operating margin (TTM)
description: TTM operating income divided by TTM total revenue (four quarterly statements), times 100; falls back to latest annual when four quarters are unavailable, with the basis recorded in ebit_margin_basis. Not Yahoo's single-quarter operatingMargins.
calculation: Operating profit ÷ revenue × 100 (trailing twelve months from four quarters; latest annual as fallback).
interpretation: Higher = more of each sales dollar kept as operating profit. Stable high margins signal pricing power and efficiency.
applicability: Breaks for pre-revenue firms (revenue ≈ 0 → explodes); means something different for financials.
gloss: Operating profit as share of sales (TTM)
analogy: For every dollar of sales, this is the slice kept as operating profit before interest and taxes.
learn: Operating margin measures how much profit is left from each dollar of sales after operating costs, before interest and taxes. This figure divides Operating Income by Total Revenue, both summed across the last four quarters: a trailing twelve-month (TTM) margin, not Yahoo's single-quarter snapshot.

label: Rev growth YoY (quarter)
description: Latest reported quarter revenue versus the same quarter a year ago (ticker.info revenueGrowth, times 100).
calculation: Latest quarter revenue vs the same quarter a year ago (Yahoo revenueGrowth × 100).
interpretation: Higher = faster top-line growth, but growth ≠ health (a company can grow into losses). Single quarter, so noisy.
applicability: Distorted by tiny prior-year bases (micro-caps, commodity ramps → huge % off a small base).
gloss: Sales growth vs same quarter last year
analogy: Compared with a year ago: is the business growing, flat, or shrinking?
learn: Year-over-year (YoY) growth compares revenue in the latest reported quarter with the same quarter one year ago (Yahoo revenueGrowth). One quarter can be noisy, so look for a pattern over time when you dig deeper. Growing sales alone does not mean a healthy business: a company can grow revenue while losing money, so it is worth checking margins and cash flow too. A small prior-year base can also inflate the percentage sharply, so a very large number here does not always mean strong momentum.

label: Net debt / EBITDA
description: Net debt (info_net_debt, or info_total_debt minus info_total_cash) divided by Yahoo EBITDA; periods may differ. A rough leverage signal, not a precise accounting ratio.
calculation: (Total debt − cash) ÷ EBITDA: roughly how many years of earnings to clear net debt.
interpretation: Lower = less leverage, safer. Negative = net cash. High = exposed in downturns or when rates rise.
applicability: Meaningless for financials ("cash" includes customer/policyholder assets); explodes when EBITDA ≈ 0 (distressed/pre-profit).
analogy: If operating profit stayed steady, about how many years to repay net debt from cash generation?
learn: Net debt is total debt minus cash on hand (Yahoo). EBITDA is Yahoo's reported EBITDA figure, often trailing and not necessarily matched to the same instant as the balance sheet. Use this as a rough leverage signal, not a precise accounting ratio.

label: FCF margin (annual)
description: Free cash flow divided by total revenue (latest annual cash flow and income statements), times 100.
calculation: Free cash flow ÷ revenue × 100 (latest annual statements).
interpretation: Higher = more real cash per sales dollar, harder to fake than accounting profit. The strongest single health signal.
applicability: Breaks for pre-revenue firms (revenue ≈ 0); not meaningful for financials.
gloss: Free cash left from each sales dollar (latest annual statements)
analogy: After running the business, how much cash is left from each sales dollar, not the same as accounting profit.
learn: Free cash flow (FCF) is cash left after running and investing in the business. This card computes FCF margin from the latest annual cash flow and income statements, not Yahoo's trailing Key Statistics ratio. Run the metric audit script to compare.

label: Debt / equity
description: Total borrowings relative to shareholders' equity (the owners' stake), from the latest annual balance sheet.
calculation: Total debt ÷ shareholders' equity (latest annual balance sheet).
interpretation: Lower = less borrowed money per dollar of owners' capital, so more cushion in a downturn. Higher = more leverage, riskier when profits dip or rates rise.
applicability: Distorted when equity is thin or negative: heavy buybacks can push equity below zero, and the ratio then flips or explodes and stops being meaningful. Not shown for banks.
analogy: Like comparing a mortgage to home equity: how much of the company is borrowed versus owned.
learn: Debt-to-equity divides total debt by shareholders' equity (the owners' stake) from the latest annual balance sheet. It is a second read on leverage alongside Net debt / EBITDA: how heavily the company leans on borrowing versus its own capital. Read a very high number, or negative equity, with care.

label: Current ratio
description: Current assets relative to current liabilities, from the latest annual balance sheet: short-term resources against short-term bills.
calculation: Current assets ÷ current liabilities (latest annual balance sheet).
interpretation: Above 1 means short-term assets cover short-term bills. Higher = more comfortable near-term liquidity; below 1 can signal a cash crunch.
applicability: Not defined for banks: their balance sheet has no current/non-current split. A very high ratio is not automatically good, since it can mean cash sitting idle.
analogy: Like checking your savings against next month's bills: can the company cover what is due soon?
learn: The current ratio divides current assets (cash and things convertible to cash within a year) by current liabilities (bills due within a year), from the latest annual balance sheet. Above 1 means near-term resources cover near-term obligations, though a very high ratio can mean cash sitting idle instead of being put to work. Banks do not report this split, so it shows only for operating companies.

label: Return on equity
description: Profit earned on owners' equity: profit belonging to common shareholders divided by their equity stake, from the latest annual statements.
calculation: Net income to common stockholders ÷ shareholders' equity × 100 (latest annual statements; period-end equity).
interpretation: Higher = more profit generated per dollar of owners' capital. A durable high ROE points to an efficient, profitable business.
applicability: Misleads when equity is thin or negative: a loss over negative equity can read as a spuriously positive percentage. Uses profit to common shareholders and period-end equity; Yahoo averages equity across the year instead, so it differs from Yahoo's ROE by design. Means something different for banks.
analogy: Like the interest rate the business earns on the capital shareholders have invested.
learn: Return on equity (ROE) divides profit attributable to common shareholders by their equity stake, from the latest annual statements. It asks: for each dollar owners have in the business, how much profit did it earn this year? We use period-end equity, so it can differ from Yahoo's averaged figure. Watch out when equity is very small or negative: a loss divided by negative equity can come out positive, looking like strong profitability when it is not.

label: Price / tangible book
description: Market value relative to tangible book value (equity minus goodwill and other intangibles), from the latest annual balance sheet.
calculation: Market cap ÷ tangible book value (latest annual balance sheet).
interpretation: Lower = you pay less per dollar of hard, tangible net worth. For banks it is a core valuation yardstick; below 1 can signal doubts about asset quality.
applicability: Tangible book value is equity minus goodwill and other intangibles, a key yardstick for banks. Not shown when intangibles exceed equity (tangible book zero or negative): the ratio would be meaningless.
analogy: Like paying for a house versus its rebuild-from-scratch value: how far above (or below) the tangible net worth is the price?
learn: Tangible book value strips goodwill and other intangibles out of shareholders' equity, leaving the hard net worth. Price-to-tangible-book divides market value by that figure. Banks are valued heavily on this: near or below 1 means the market is cautious about the balance sheet.

label: Net margin
description: Bottom-line profit (after everything) as a percent of revenue, from the latest annual statements.
interpretation: Higher = more of each revenue dollar survives to the bottom line after all costs, interest, and taxes.
applicability: Profit after everything ÷ revenue. For a bank, "revenue" is net interest plus fees, so read this as overall profitability, not operating efficiency. Breaks for pre-revenue firms (revenue ≈ 0).
analogy: Of every dollar that comes in, how many cents are left as final profit after all the bills.
learn: Net margin divides bottom-line net income by revenue. Unlike operating margin, it is after interest and taxes too: the final slice kept. For banks, where "revenue" means net interest income plus fees, it reads as overall profitability.

label: Return on assets
description: Profit earned on the company's total assets: total net income over total assets, from the latest annual statements.
calculation: Net income ÷ total assets × 100 (latest annual statements; period-end assets).
interpretation: Higher = more profit squeezed from each dollar of assets. For banks, which sit on huge asset bases, it is a core efficiency gauge.
applicability: A core efficiency gauge for banks (they run on huge asset bases). Uses total profit ÷ total assets, whereas Return on equity uses profit belonging to common shareholders ÷ their equity: the two "return" metrics use different profit lines by design. Period-end assets, not Yahoo's averaged figure.
analogy: Like the yield a business earns on everything it owns, not just the owners' slice.
learn: Return on assets divides total profit by total assets (from the latest annual statements). It answers: for every dollar of assets, how much profit? Banks live on this because they operate enormous balance sheets. Note it uses total net income, while Return on equity uses profit belonging to common shareholders: different profit lines by design.

label: Dividend yield
description: Annual dividend as a percent of the share price (Yahoo dividendYield, already in percent).
calculation: Annual dividend per share ÷ share price × 100 (Yahoo dividendYield).
interpretation: Higher = more cash returned per dollar invested. A very high yield can mean a falling price or a payout under strain, not just generosity.
applicability: Cash paid to shareholders as a percent of the share price. A very high yield can flag a falling price or a payout at risk, not just generosity. Absent when the company pays no dividend.
analogy: Like the interest a savings account pays, except the dividend can be cut and the share price moves.
learn: Dividend yield is the annual dividend divided by the share price. It is the cash income a share throws off, before any price change. A high yield can simply mean the price fell, or that the payout is at risk, not generosity.

label: Net cash vs price
description: Net cash (cash minus debt) as a fraction of the market price (market cap), from the latest balance sheet.
interpretation: Higher = more of the market price is backed by spare cash. Above 1 means the company holds more net cash than its whole market price: it is trading below its cash.
applicability: Cash minus debt, divided by the company's market price (market cap). A cushion for a company not yet profitable. Goes negative when debt exceeds cash (a net-debt position).
gloss: Net cash as a share of the market price
analogy: Like buying something and finding a chunk of the price is just cash in the drawer.
learn: For a company that is not profitable yet, cash is the lifeline. This divides its net cash (cash minus debt) by its market price. A high figure, especially above 1, means a large share of the price, or more than all of it, is simply cash on the balance sheet. Higher is safer here.

label: Working capital
description: Short-term assets minus short-term liabilities, from the latest annual balance sheet: the near-term cash cushion.
calculation: Current assets − current liabilities (latest annual balance sheet).
interpretation: Positive = the company can cover its near-term bills with near-term assets. Negative = a possible short-term squeeze.
applicability: Short-term assets minus short-term bills, from the latest balance sheet. Positive = a near-term cushion; negative = a possible squeeze. Not defined for banks.
analogy: Like your bank balance minus the bills due this month: what is left to work with.
learn: Working capital is current assets (cash and things turning to cash within a year) minus current liabilities (bills due within a year). It is the short-term cushion that keeps a young company running between funding rounds. Shown as a money amount.

label: Cash runway
description: How many months the company's cash would last at its current cash burn, from the latest annual statements.
calculation: Cash on hand ÷ monthly cash burn (12 months of burn), in months.
interpretation: Higher = more months before the cash runs out at today's spending. A short runway means the company likely needs to raise money soon.
applicability: Only for companies burning cash. Cash on hand ÷ average monthly cash burn. Assumes the burn holds steady, though a real company's can change fast.
gloss: Months of cash left at the current burn
analogy: Like dividing your savings by your monthly spending to see how many months you can go without new income.
learn: Cash runway estimates how long the company can keep operating before it runs out of cash, at its current burn rate: cash on hand divided by the average monthly cash outflow. For a pre-revenue company this is the survival clock: a short runway means new funding is needed soon. It assumes the burn rate holds steady, which rarely happens exactly.

label: Cash burn (monthly)
description: Average cash the company spends each month (operating cash flow plus capital spending, over 12 months), from the latest annual statements.
calculation: −(operating cash flow + capital spending) ÷ 12 (a monthly amount).
interpretation: Higher = the company is spending cash faster, so the runway is shorter. Shown only when the company is burning cash.
applicability: Average monthly cash outflow (operating cash flow plus capital spending, over 12 months). Shown only when the company is burning cash.
analogy: Like your monthly spending: the faster it goes, the sooner the savings run out.
learn: Burn rate is the average cash a company spends each month after running and investing in the business: operating cash flow plus capital spending, spread over the year. Paired with cash on hand it sets the runway. Shown as a money amount per month.
